strengths: Introduces a timely and practically relevant task: language-driven spatio-temporal scenario mining for autonomous driving logs, with explicit localization of referred objects in 3D and time rather than only text answers or static grounding.

RefAV is potentially useful as a benchmark: it builds on Argoverse 2 sensor data with 10 Hz 3D tracks, HD maps, multimodal inputs, 10,000 prompts, negative examples, and related-object annotations, which together target dynamic multi-agent interactions better than many existing RMOT/VQA datasets.

The paper provides clear baseline families and a sensible set of metrics, including HOTA-Temporal, HOTA-Track, log balanced accuracy, and timestamp balanced accuracy. The results show a meaningful gap between simple class/CLIP/GroundingDINO-style baselines and the program-synthesis approach.

The implementation appendix is comparatively detailed, including tracker formats, prompting details, post-processing, and an API listing, which improves reproducibility if the promised code, dataset, and tracker outputs are actually released.
weaknesses: The strongest concern is benchmark-method circularity. About 9,880 of 10,000 expressions are procedurally defined from the same style of atomic functions/API that RefProg later uses for inference. This can make RefProg well matched to the label-generation process rather than demonstrating robust natural-language scenario mining in the wild.

Dataset validity is underdocumented. The paper says generated scenarios are manually verified, but does not specify annotator count, quality-control protocol, inter-annotator agreement, rejection rates, or how many generated positives were checked. Given that the benchmark is mostly synthetic/procedural, these details are material rather than presentation-only.

The evaluation is narrower than the framing suggests. Despite discussing recent VLMs, the main non-program baselines are class filtering, GroundingDINO/SAM inflation, and CLIP track classification; there is no strong modern multimodal video/3D VLM baseline adapted to the task, so the claim that off-the-shelf VLMs fail is only partially supported.

The dataset is limited by AV2 scale and coverage: only 1000 short logs, Pittsburgh-centered data, clipped practical range, no native traffic-light/weather/lighting labels, and only 120 manually defined expressions. This limits conclusions about safety-critical long-tail mining in broader fleet data.

Some design choices may inflate or obscure performance. RefClassify thresholds are grouped by prompt using positive and negative examples, RefProg applies timestamp dilation and track filtering before evaluation, and all methods are ultimately evaluated on downsampled 2 Hz outputs despite the benchmark motivation emphasizing 10 Hz annotations.

The paper does not clearly describe train/validation/test splits or whether prompts/logs/scenario templates are disjoint across splits. Without this, it is hard to assess generalization, especially for program-synthesis methods that may exploit repeated procedural templates.

Presentation has several rough edges that affect confidence: inconsistent naming such as RefGen/RefClass versus RefInflate/RefClassify, typos in tables and appendix text, and an incomplete-feeling contributions paragraph. These are fixable, but they compound the more substantive concerns about dataset construction and evaluation scope.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: language-driven spatio-temporal scenario mining for autonomous driving logs, with localization of referred objects in 3D and time rather than only scene-level answers.
Building on Argoverse 2 gives the benchmark useful multimodal context, HD maps, 30 object categories, and higher-frequency 10 Hz tracks, which are well motivated for dynamic multi-agent interactions.

The paper provides several baseline families and reports multiple metrics, including temporal tracking metrics and log/timestamp balanced accuracy. The RefProg results clearly show that simple class filtering, CLIP-style track classification, and 2D grounding-to-3D inflation are insufficient for this task.

The appendix includes nontrivial implementation details, the LLM prompt for program synthesis, tracker input format, and the API listing, which helps reproducibility if the promised code and dataset are released.
weaknesses: The central benchmark has a serious circularity concern: 9,880 of 10,000 expressions are procedurally defined from a hand-crafted API, and the strongest baseline, RefProg, uses essentially the same API/program-synthesis paradigm to solve the task. This makes the headline gains difficult to interpret as general language/vision reasoning rather than recovery of the dataset generation DSL from generated prompts.

The annotation quality evidence is inadequate for a dataset paper. The manuscript states that generated scenarios and videos are manually verified, but does not report annotator counts, acceptance/rejection rates after manual review, inter-annotator agreement, error rates on a held-out audit, or how ambiguous prompts are resolved. This is especially concerning because the authors themselves identify common LLM generation errors such as reversed relationships and underspecified code.

The evaluation is narrow and favors the proposed formulation. There are no trained or fine-tuned baselines, no comparison to recent 3D VLM/grounding systems beyond simple repurposed pipelines, and no split-wise or category-wise analysis showing whether performance holds on manually defined, weather/lighting, rare, negative, or out-of-API scenarios.

The negative examples appear to be randomly sampled log-prompt pairs, which may make log-level retrieval substantially easier than realistic hard-negative scenario mining. The paper does not analyze hard negatives, near misses, or semantically similar prompts that differ in temporal or relational details.

The work claims a 10 Hz benchmark for fine-grained motion, but the baseline outputs are downsampled to 2 Hz for evaluation, and the sampling-rate ablation suggests limited sensitivity of HOTA-Temporal to 2 Hz vs 10 Hz. This weakens a major motivation relative to nuScenes-style datasets.

RefProg is not really an end-to-end vision-language model over raw sensor data; it relies on offline 3D tracks and map/geometry functions, and explicitly does not use image/LiDAR information after tracking. The framing around VLMs and raw multimodal scenario mining sometimes overstates what is demonstrated.

The metric definitions and results raise interpretability questions. For example, even with ground-truth tracks RefProg reaches only 64.8 HOTA-Temporal, while all-ground-truth-tracks balanced accuracy is 50.0, but the paper does not deeply diagnose whether errors come from program synthesis, metric design, annotation noise, or prompt ambiguity.

Reproducibility remains partly fragile because core dataset generation and best baseline performance rely on proprietary LLMs such as Claude and Gemini, and the paper does not give enough detail about manual edits, generated-code verification, or exact dataset construction decisions to independently recreate the benchmark.

Presentation has many polish issues that distract from confidence in the work, including malformed spacing, typos, inconsistent names such as RefGen/RefClass, duplicated words, section numbering that skips 4.4, and noisy appendix API text. These are not decisive alone, but they reinforce concerns about benchmark precision.

strengths: The paper identifies a well-motivated and timely problem: language-driven spatio-temporal scenario mining for autonomous driving logs, with outputs requiring 3D object tracks and temporal localization rather than only text answers or single-frame grounding.

RefAV is a useful benchmark contribution. It contains 10K natural-language prompts over 1000 Argoverse 2 logs, includes negative prompts, uses 10 Hz 3D tracks, and targets dynamic multi-agent interactions that are underrepresented in prior RMOT/VQA datasets.

The task formulation and metrics are largely appropriate. HOTA-Temporal, HOTA-Track, log balanced accuracy, and timestamp balanced accuracy separate localization, association, and retrieval behavior in a way that matches the stated scenario-mining goal.

The experimental results are informative: simple class filtering, CLIP-based track classification, 2D-to-3D inflation, and RefProg establish a meaningful baseline ladder. The large gap between RefProg and the other zero-shot baselines supports the claim that compositional temporal reasoning is difficult for off-the-shelf VLM-style methods.

The paper is unusually transparent about limitations and implementation details. The appendix gives prompts, tracker post-processing, API functions, related/other-object evaluation, sampling-rate ablations, and dataset statistics, which improves reproducibility if the promised code and data are released.
weaknesses: The main scientific concern is circularity between dataset construction and the strongest method. Most labels are procedurally generated from the same kind of atomic-function API that RefProg later uses for prediction, so RefProg may be advantaged by matching the latent annotation language rather than demonstrating general language-grounded scenario understanding.

The dataset’s semantic validity is not fully quantified. The paper states that generated scenarios and videos are manually verified, but does not report inter-annotator agreement, acceptance/rejection rates, the fraction of clips fully checked, or residual label-noise estimates. This matters because 9880 of 10K expressions are procedurally defined and only 120 are manually defined.

The benchmark is constrained by Argoverse 2 and by the available program primitives. The authors acknowledge missing traffic-light state, limited weather/lighting annotations, and finite API coverage; as a result, many safety-relevant scenarios may be absent or only weakly represented.

The empirical comparison is somewhat narrow. The baselines are useful, but there is no evaluation of fine-tuned models, modern video/multimodal LLMs with temporal prompting, retrieval-oriented baselines over BEV/track features, or methods trained on part of RefAV. Thus the results establish difficulty and a strong program baseline, but not a broad picture of the modeling frontier.

Some metric results need clearer interpretation. For example, the all-ground-truth-tracks oracle has only 13.3 HOTA-Temporal and 50% balanced accuracy, and HOTA-Temporal/Track values depend heavily on timestamp labeling and dilation choices. The paper explains the metrics, but more qualitative error analysis tied to these numbers would make the evidence stronger.

Reproducibility depends on external proprietary or changing components, especially Claude/Gemini calls for scenario generation and RefProg. The paper provides prompts, but exact LLM behavior, version availability, and cost/runtime may be difficult to reproduce over time.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and useful benchmark for natural-language scenario mining in autonomous driving logs, targeting spatio-temporal localization of multi-agent interactions rather than only static referring expressions or VQA-style answers.

RefAV is built on AV2 with 360-degree cameras, LiDAR, HD maps, 30 object classes, and 10 Hz track annotations, which is a strong foundation for evaluating fine-grained motion and planning-centric scenarios.

The dataset design includes negative prompts, temporal localization, related-object annotations, weather/lighting attributes, and examples involving rare or safety-relevant interactions; these make the benchmark more realistic than many prior RMOT/VQA datasets.

The paper provides several meaningful baselines and ablations, including class filtering, image/text embedding methods, ReferGPT, black-box LLM use, RefProg, multiple trackers, different LLMs, sampling-rate analysis, token/cost analysis, and transfer to nuPrompt.

RefProg is a simple but effective baseline: program synthesis over an atomic spatio-temporal API substantially outperforms the other zero-shot baselines on RefAV, and the failure-case analysis usefully identifies remaining limitations.

The manuscript is mostly clear about the dataset generation pipeline and includes implementation details, prompts, API listings, and qualitative examples that should help reproducibility if the promised code and dataset are released.
weaknesses: A central concern is dataset-method coupling: most examples are procedurally generated using the same style of atomic functions that RefProg later uses for inference. Even with manual verification, this may bias the benchmark toward program-synthesis methods and understate the difficulty for methods that do not share the hidden compositional grammar.

The dataset scale is somewhat overstated. It has 10,000 log-prompt pairs but only 407 unique scenario descriptions, and 9,880 of 10,000 examples are procedurally defined. This limits evidence that the benchmark covers the long tail of natural language users would write in practice.

Annotation quality control is not fully characterized. The paper reports 200 hours of verification, but does not provide inter-annotator agreement, systematic label-noise estimates, rejection rates after manual review, or detailed evidence that all positive/negative pairs and temporal boundaries were validated consistently.

The strongest method is not very vision-centric: RefProg primarily reasons over off-the-shelf 3D tracks, maps, and hand-crafted motion predicates, and the appendix states it does not explicitly rely on LiDAR or cameras during filtering. This is useful for scenario mining, but the contribution is closer to structured query/program synthesis over tracks than a general VLM-based perception model.

Some empirical claims need more caution. The nuPrompt comparison may conflate language grounding gains with a stronger underlying tracker/decoder, and the claim of outperforming trained state-of-the-art methods is not clearly apples-to-apples.

The evaluation of modern VLMs is limited. The paper shows that naive image-embedding/captioning and black-box LLM approaches struggle, but it does not evaluate trained or fine-tuned multimodal video/3D models on RefAV, so broad claims about VLM limitations should be framed as limitations of the tested zero-shot adaptations.

Reproducibility depends heavily on proprietary and evolving LLMs/APIs such as GPT-5, Claude, and Gemini. The paper includes prompts and cost statistics, but exact behavior may be hard to reproduce, and the dataset generation process itself used proprietary models plus manual edits.

The manuscript has notable presentation issues, including apparent placeholder text around the challenge description, typos, and some awkward/incomplete phrasing. These do not invalidate the contribution, but they reduce confidence in polish and careful reporting.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: natural-language scenario mining in autonomous-driving logs with temporal and 3D localization, which is more planning-relevant than many existing referring-expression benchmarks.
RefAV has useful scale and modalities: 10k log-query pairs over AV2 with 10 Hz tracks, 360-degree cameras, LiDAR, maps, negative prompts, and labels for referred/related/other objects.

The empirical results are informative in showing that simple class filtering, CLIP-style image similarity, ReferGPT, and black-box LLM use perform poorly, while structured program synthesis is substantially stronger.

The appendices provide some practical implementation details, prompt templates, token/cost accounting, examples of generated programs, and additional statistics, which improves reproducibility relative to many LLM-based benchmark papers.
weaknesses: The most serious issue is benchmark circularity. Most labels are procedurally generated from a hand-written API, and the proposed RefProg method uses essentially the same style of hand-written atomic functions to solve the benchmark. This makes the strong RefProg results hard to interpret as evidence of general scenario understanding rather than recovery of the dataset-generation grammar.

The dataset’s apparent scale is misleading: the appendix reports only 407 unique scenario descriptions, with 9880 procedurally defined and only 120 manually defined expressions. This limits linguistic diversity and weakens the claim that the benchmark measures open-ended natural-language scenario mining.

Annotation quality is insufficiently supported. The paper says scenarios are manually verified/edited, but it does not report inter-annotator agreement, validation sampling error, disagreement resolution, failure rates after correction, or an independent audit of final labels. Given the synthetic-code origin of the labels, this is a material concern.

The method contribution is modest. RefProg is largely a program-synthesis wrapper around pre-existing 3D tracks and a manually designed API, closely related to prior visual-programming approaches. Its novelty lies more in adapting this recipe to AV logs than in a new vision or learning method.

The task definition claims raw RGB/LiDAR/map scenario mining, but RefProg largely operates on tracker outputs and handcrafted geometric predicates; it explicitly does not rely on LiDAR/cameras except through offline perception, and its own failure analysis notes poor support for weather/lighting prompts despite these being part of the dataset.

The evaluation is not broad enough to establish generality. Most comparisons are zero-shot baselines, and there is no learned baseline trained on RefAV, no evaluation on independently human-written queries, and limited analysis of whether performance transfers beyond the API-generated prompt distribution.

The nuPrompt comparison is not fully convincing as a state-of-the-art claim. RefProg uses a different tracker/decoder setup and task adaptation, making it unclear how much improvement comes from the program-synthesis language grounding versus stronger underlying tracking/perception components.

Several metrics and tables are confusing or underexplained. For example, the 'Ground Truth' row has HOTA 100 but low HOTA-Temporal/HOTA-Track, and the implications of these oracle rows are not easy to interpret. This hurts clarity and makes it harder to assess whether the benchmark rewards the intended behavior.

Reproducibility depends heavily on proprietary or time-varying LLM APIs such as Claude and GPT-5, plus prompt behavior and code execution details. Although prompts are included, exact reproducibility and long-term comparability are uncertain.

The writing has presentation issues that suggest insufficient polish: broken phrases around the challenge description, typos, awkward formatting, and dense tables. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they compound the clarity problems.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important problem: language-driven spatio-temporal scenario mining for autonomous driving logs, with localization of referred objects over both time and 3D space rather than only text answers or static grounding.

RefAV is a meaningful benchmark contribution. It leverages AV2's 10 Hz tracks, HD maps, 360-degree sensors, negative prompts, weather/lighting labels, and multi-agent interactions, filling a gap between RMOT, VQA, and planning-centric AV evaluation.

The dataset construction process is described in useful detail, including the atomic-function pipeline, manual verification, annotation effort, examples of common LLM generation errors, and additional appendix statistics. This supports reproducibility and helps users understand likely label characteristics.

The empirical study is broad for a benchmark paper: class filtering, CLIP/image similarity, ReferGPT, black-box LLM use, RefProg, different detectors, different LLMs, related/other object analysis, sampling-rate analysis, and a nuPrompt transfer experiment are all considered.

The main result is convincing at the level of establishing task difficulty and showing that simple VLM repurposing is insufficient. RefProg with predicted tracks substantially improves over the strongest non-program baseline on HOTA-Temporal, and the ground-truth-track result shows that language/temporal reasoning remains a major bottleneck independent of tracking quality.

The method is simple and useful as a strong baseline. Program synthesis over interpretable motion/map primitives is well matched to the task and provides a practical, inspectable alternative to opaque end-to-end VLM prompting.
weaknesses: The largest concern is benchmark-method coupling. Most RefAV examples are procedurally defined through an atomic API, while RefProg solves the task by synthesizing programs over a similar atomic API. Even with manual verification, this may bias the benchmark toward API-compositional methods and overstate general scenario-mining generality relative to freer-form human queries.

The dataset is sizable in log-prompt pairs but less diverse than the headline number suggests: the appendix reports 407 unique scenario descriptions, 9880 procedurally defined examples, and only 120 manually defined examples. This limits claims about broad natural-language diversity and real open-ended scenario mining.

RefProg's core reasoning uses tracks, maps, and hand-engineered motion primitives rather than directly reasoning from raw RGB/LiDAR, despite the task framing emphasizing raw multimodal logs. This is a reasonable baseline design, but the paper sometimes blurs the distinction between evaluating scenario mining from sensor data and evaluating language/program filtering on top of existing 3D tracking.

The negative examples are partly randomly sampled and may not be as hard as realistic near-miss negatives. More adversarial negatives, paraphrase splits, or held-out scenario families would better test whether models understand scenario semantics rather than matching common templates.

The nuPrompt comparison is encouraging but not fully conclusive as a cross-dataset validation of RefProg. The setting changes detector/backbone choices and removes map-dependent functions, so the comparison to trained methods may conflate language reasoning gains with differences in perception inputs or evaluation setup.

Reproducibility depends on proprietary or rapidly changing LLMs such as Claude/GPT/Gemini, and some reported costs/token counts are tied to future API/pricing assumptions. Open-model results are included but much weaker, so exact replication may be difficult.

There are noticeable presentation issues, including incomplete challenge placeholders/links and awkward extracted text around the competition paragraph. These are not fatal, but they reduce polish for a conference submission.
